prompt: Use case: illustration-story. Asset type: a production atlas of circular illustrated tokens for Creation, an original elemental myth about making a vast living world. The reference is the APPROVED STYLE AND CONTINUITY anchor, not a sheet to copy unchanged. Paint new subjects in exactly that family: luminous opaque gouache, selective fine ink contours, strong simplified silhouettes readable at 64px; deep lapis interiors, jade and turquoise, burnt ochre, muted coral, warm ivory light, very narrow ivory-gold rims. Not glossy coins or flat generic pictograms. Each icon is a complete perfect CIRCLE with opaque painted interior and transparent empty space outside. Center each circle in its own equal grid cell, circle diameter 80 percent of the shorter cell side, generous empty gutters. Absolutely no letters, names, numbers, grid lines, labels, UI, watermark or cast shadows outside circles. No modern laboratory hardware, books, houses or buildings. Only the specified object inside each circle, with a simple dark ground or essential local context. Tiny details must not carry the meaning. Related states should differ in structure, not merely colour. Follow item order exactly, left to right, top to bottom. Exactly 20 circles in 5 columns and 4 rows. Landscape atlas. Exact cell subjects: CELL 1, Social group: Four related tree dwellers share a sheltered branch network: one looks outward, one attends to a juvenile and two face each other at close range, with relaxed but alert postures. Distinguish: Sustained group relationships and care, without a specific alarm, human symbolic conversation or simple climbing pair. CELL 2, Language: Two human figures in profile face one another with open speaking mouths and different deliberate hand gestures, while a third follows their shared gaze toward a small carved-free stone and the Moon. Distinguish: Reciprocal human symbolic communication, not one animal call, storytelling scene or evidence review; no text, speech bubbles or alphabet. CELL 3, Story: A seated human narrator gestures to two listeners; behind the moving hand, a soft ochre vignette shows a small animal travelling beneath a crescent Moon, clearly separate from the present ground. Distinguish: Narration evokes an imagined or remembered sequence in open space, not a painted wall, book or direct lesson at the shore. CELL 4, Constellations: Seven ivory stars form a loose animal-like pattern across ultramarine darkness, joined by a few fine ochre lines; unrelated background stars remain unconnected. Distinguish: Selected stars connected into a pattern, not every star linked, a painted rock surface or counting device. CELL 5, Calendar: A human observer crouches beside four small groups of counting pebbles and incised tally strokes on a natural stone, beneath a repeated star pattern shown at four seasonal positions around a single horizon. Distinguish: Deliberate record of recurring sky and season, not a modern calendar page, clock or mere cycle of leaves. CELL 6, Wonder: A small human figure stands on the hooked shore with head tipped far back and both arms gently open beneath a vast cluster of luminous stars; the upward gaze dominates. Distinguish: Receptive astonishment at the sky, without a pointing exchange, counting marks or joined stellar figure. CELL 7, Question: One human figure extends an open palm toward a small bright Moon while turning an expectant face toward another person; the other person's hand pauses above the empty space between them. Distinguish: An unresolved shared inquiry shown by reciprocal pose and open space, without written question marks or a proposed sky-sea connection. CELL 8, Lunar rhythm: Four small phases of the same paired-crater Moon arc above two alternating shore strips, one with a broad high-low tidal range and one with a narrower range. Distinguish: Repeated Moon phases tied to alternating tidal range, not a solitary crescent or a simple high-low pair. CELL 9, Lunar hypothesis: A human observer points one hand toward the pale Moon and the other toward two tidal bands on the familiar hooked shore; one fine tentative ochre arc joins those observed features. Distinguish: A proposed connection is the foreground action, without future date markers or measured confirmation; the arc is a visual conjecture convention. CELL 10, Spring-tide prediction: Beside the familiar shore, a person sets two pale dry ochre marks far apart on a rock face while indicating an outlined future full Moon above a short pebble count; the present sea remains between the marks. Distinguish: Dry proposed upper and lower limits and a future full-Moon cue, not an already wet verified tide record. CELL 11, Observed spring tide: At the same marked shore, one observer compares a clear dark high-water stain with the newly exposed low-water edge below it; the widely separated ochre marks now align with those two observed levels beneath a full Moon. Distinguish: Actual wet stain and exposed low water establish a checked range; keep the prediction rock and marks identical. CELL 12, Shared discovery: Three people stand at the same marked tidal rock; one indicates the high-water stain and low-water edge while another compares the pebble record and a third looks between the evidence and Moon. Distinguish: Peers share a tested observation and its record, without a single observer or an adult-to-child lesson. CELL 13, Night vision: A nocturnal furred animal's large forward eyes reflect pale moonlight above a dark branch, with its whiskered face and the branch still readable in a nearly black jade setting. Distinguish: Paired low-light eyes in an active nocturnal animal, not the Moon granting vision or one isolated marine eye. CELL 14, Pigment: Three small wet daubs of ochre, coral and dark mineral color sit on a flat natural stone beside a crushed mineral fragment and a short watery smear. Distinguish: Prepared wet coloring material, without a vessel, modern palette, loose soil or completed picture. CELL 15, Cave painting: The established sea cave's dry pale upper wall bears one simple ochre animal outline and a hand stencil, with a human hand adding a broad mark; the dark wave-washed entrance remains below. Distinguish: Clearly handmade picture on dry rock depicting a plausible animal, not a real creature, fossil or celestial mural. CELL 16, Imagined beast: On the same dry cave wall, an ochre painted creature combines a long-tailed mammal body, branching antlers and feathered wings in one impossible silhouette; a small painter's hand remains at the edge. Distinguish: Impossible anatomy is visibly a painting, never a resurrected sauropod or a newly living lineage. CELL 17, Echo: A lone human calls inside the established sea cave; one pale sound arc travels toward the curved dry wall and a fainter matching arc returns toward the caller, with the sea visible through the lower opening. Distinguish: Opposing original and reflected sound paths in the same rocky chamber, not multiple singers or a composed melodic pattern. CELL 18, Chorus: Three human singers of different heights face inward on the dry cave ledge, their mouths open and three separate pale sound ribbons meeting in one repeating arc above them. Distinguish: Several people singing together, with distinct contributors and shared pattern; no written music or speech bubbles. CELL 19, Painted sky: The same dry pale cave wall carries a bold ultramarine patch filled with oversized ochre stars, an impossible coral spiral and a pale crescent; a painted handprint marks the lower edge. Distinguish: Clearly pigment on rock with deliberately impossible celestial arrangement, not a natural starfield or an astronomical record. CELL 20, Teaching: An older person traces the familiar Moon-and-tide pattern in sand beside the marked shore while two younger listeners follow the hand; their faces and hands form a close triangle around the evidence. Distinguish: Knowledge passed across generations using the already tested shore, not a modern classroom, book or peer-only discussion. Keep the common circle size and painted finish. Anatomical lineages matter: insects have six legs, birds feathered wings, bats membranous finger-supported wings. A depicted early cell is a symbolic magnified view, not a modern laboratory slide. The world is not Earth's recognizable map. People, if listed, have varied warm earth-brown complexions, simplified features and no modern objects. Never add people, plants or animals to a subject that predates them. Do not draw the subject names.
